disease_info: Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by persistent restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, an intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, and disturbances in how one experiences body weight or shape. It often begins in adolescence or young adulthood but can emerge or recur later in life, sometimes around major life transitions, illness, or losses. The course can be chronic or relapsing, with medical complications affecting multiple organ systems and significant psychosocial impairment, even when the person denies the severity. It is distinguished from other eating disorders by the combination of underweight status and the centrality of weight, shape, or weight-gain fears in the person’s self-evaluation and behavior.

narrative.stressor: William’s eating problems began to emerge insidiously after his wife died suddenly from a stroke three years ago, an event that shattered the orderly home life he had relied on as a counterbalance to decades of stressful police work. At first he simply "wasn’t hungry" and skipped meals while throwing himself into overtime shifts, but over time he began to view his increasingly strict, minimalist eating as a way to exert control and discipline in a life that felt otherwise empty and chaotic. Colleagues noticed he no longer joined them for shared meals, and family gatherings with traditional Mexican dishes became rare as he insisted on cooking separate, sparse portions for himself, framing it as "keeping in shape" for the job even as his uniform sizes dropped and he grew more withdrawn. He finally came to psychiatric attention after a routine department physical flagged his significantly low weight and abnormal labs, and his primary care physician urged a mental health evaluation when William admitted he was terrified that eating more would make him "soft" and unable to manage without his late wife.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m scared that if I start eating more, I’ll lose control and put on weight I can’t afford at my age and in my line of work.”

narrative.stressor: As Maria approached retirement from her long-term job as a building cleaner, she found the looming change unsettling, worrying about losing her routines, income, and sense of usefulness. Around the same time, her doctor mentioned that her blood pressure and cholesterol were "borderline," and she began trimming portions and skipping meals, telling herself she was just trying to "be healthier" for retirement and to avoid becoming a burden on her family. What began as modest dieting gradually turned into rigid food rules that clashed with her usual joy in cooking and sharing traditional Puerto Rican meals, leaving her increasingly isolated at family gatherings and church events where food is central to connection. Her husband and domino friends eventually urged her to see a doctor when they noticed her clothes hanging loosely and her reluctance to eat at social events, and after her primary care physician expressed concern about her low weight and asked about her preoccupation with staying "small" in this new phase of life, she was referred for psychiatric assessment.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately all I can think about is not getting bigger as I get older, and I judge myself by what the scale says more than anything else.”

narrative.stressor: Jesus’s difficulties with eating began to escalate after he joined a highly competitive fitness challenge at his firehouse aimed at improving performance metrics and cutting response times, where body fat percentages and weigh-ins became a regular topic of locker-room comparison. Wanting to prove himself and fast-track his path to lieutenant, he started tightening his diet to "lean out" for better agility and endurance, gradually cutting out more foods and restricting his intake far beyond what his physically demanding job required. His identity as a strong, reliable firefighter became increasingly tied to staying lighter than his peers, and he began to avoid family meals and social barbecues, improvising excuses to hide how little he was actually eating even as his wife worried about how drawn and tired he looked off shift. The issue came to a head when he nearly fainted during a training drill and the department physician documented his significantly low weight, prompting a mandatory evaluation; during the consultation, he acknowledged he had been purposefully keeping his intake very low to maintain his size for work.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve been really strict about cutting back on what I eat to stay as light and quick as possible for the job, and it’s gotten out of hand.”
